outline.chapter_title: Copyright, Comedy, and the Creator Economy: Setting the Stage
outline.description: Introduces the Santos v. Kimmel dispute as a vehicle to explore modern fair use and state-law claims arising from platform-mediated content creation and late-night comedy. Frames the doctrinal stakes and the interaction among copyright, platform contracts, and fraud-based claims.
subtopics: Factual background: Cameo requests under fictitious names and broadcast on a late-night show
Claims asserted: copyright infringement, breach of contract, breach of implied contract, fraudulent inducement
Procedural posture: Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal and de novo review on appeal
Core teaching themes: transformative use in commentary/satire, market harm, pleading-stage fair use, contract enforceability through platform terms, and fraud damages

outline.chapter_title: Doctrinal Foundations of Fair Use Under 17 U.S.C. § 107
outline.description: Explains the statutory fair use framework, its purposes, and the principal factors courts assess. Highlights the evolution of the transformativeness inquiry and the role (if any) of bad faith.
subtopics: Statutory text and purposes of § 107: preservation of creativity and protection of commentary, criticism, news reporting
Four nonexclusive factors and flexible, context-specific application
Burden of proof and nature of the affirmative defense
Transformativeness after Warhol v. Goldsmith: reasonable observer, specific use-context, and limits of new meaning alone
Parody versus satire and commentary: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose and beyond
Commerciality within factor one and how it interplays with transformation
Good faith and bad faith: Harper & Row’s dictum and subsequent skepticism (Campbell; Google v. Oracle)

outline.chapter_title: Factor One in Depth: Purpose, Character, and Transformativeness
outline.description: Analyzes how courts identify the purpose and character of the secondary use and determine whether the use adds something new with a different aim or message.
subtopics: Objective versus subjective intent: reasonable observer standard and disregard of user’s or author’s subjective motives
Identifying a distinct purpose: from celebration to critique, from salesmanship to exposure
Transformative commentary on public figures and conduct versus on the work itself
Commercial late-night comedy as news/commentary: weighing criticism and humor against revenue motives
Bad faith and deception in obtaining works (e.g., pseudonyms, sting operations) and their limited role in factor one

outline.chapter_title: Factors Two and Three: Nature of the Work and Amount/Substantiality
outline.description: Explores how the creative versus factual nature of a work and publication status affect the analysis, and when copying the entirety of a work is justified for commentary or criticism, particularly in short-form videos.
subtopics: Creative versus factual works and why factor two often carries limited weight
Publication status and its significance; statutory definition of publication
Short, personalized videos: expressive content, personalization, and implications for factor two
Using the heart of the work or the whole work: necessity for commentary, criticism, or reporting
Editing, montages, and contextual framing to establish new meaning or purpose

outline.chapter_title: Factor Four: Market Harm and the Usurpation Versus Criticism Distinction
outline.description: Details the modern approach to market harm, emphasizing substitution and usurpation over reputational or criticism-related impacts. Considers potential licensing markets for critical uses.
subtopics: Hachette Book Group v. Internet Archive’s focus on competing substitutes versus devaluation through criticism
Presumptions of harm and their erosion in transformative contexts
Critical and parody uses and the unlikelihood of a viable licensing market
Assessing cognizable derivative and traditional markets in the platform age
Empirical and pleading-stage considerations in market harm allegations

outline.chapter_title: Early Adjudication of Fair Use: Motions to Dismiss and Judicial Notice
outline.description: Examines when fair use can be resolved at the pleading stage, what materials courts may consider, and the policy rationales and risks of early dismissal.
subtopics: Rule 12(b)(6) standards and the role of incorporation by reference
Judicial notice of copyright registrations and of the allegedly infringing and original works
Second Circuit guidance: TCA Television, Cariou v. Prince, and similar precedents
Policy considerations: chilling effects versus early disposition of speech-related cases
Practical tips for drafting complaints and motions with the fair use issue in mind

outline.chapter_title: Applying the Doctrine in Santos v. Kimmel
outline.description: Uses the case to illustrate factor-by-factor analysis and key points about transformativeness, deception, publication, and market harm in the late-night satire context.
subtopics: Factor one: commentary on the willingness to say absurd things for money as a different purpose
Rejecting subjective-purpose arguments and focusing on the reasonable observer
Bad faith via pseudonymous requests: limited or no role in fair use after Google v. Oracle
Factor two: published status and its limited weight
Factor three: necessity of using the whole or substantial portions to make the commentary effective
Factor four: no usurpation of Cameo’s market; criticism is not a licensable substitute
Outcome: fair use established on the pleadings

outline.description: Explores the preemption framework for state-law claims related to copyrighted works and strategic attempts to plead around the Copyright Act, even though the court resolved Santos’s state-law claims on other grounds.
subtopics: Section 301 preemption test in the Second Circuit: subject-matter and general equivalence
Melendez v. Sirius XM and the “extra element” analysis
Common state-law claims adjacent to copyright: contract, unjust enrichment, fraud, right of publicity
District court’s preemption ruling versus the Second Circuit’s decision to reach the merits
Drafting strategies and pitfalls when pleading state claims in copyright-adjacent disputes

outline.chapter_title: Platform Terms and Third-Party Beneficiary Doctrine
outline.description: Analyzes enforcement of platform Terms of Service by nonparties, with emphasis on Illinois law and drafting lessons for creator marketplaces.
subtopics: Third-party beneficiary presumption against enforcement under Illinois law
Barry v. St. Mary’s and the requirement of an express declaration of intent to benefit
Reading TOS structures: separate user and talent agreements; explicit third-party beneficiary clauses elsewhere as negative implication
Choice-of-law provisions and their strategic significance
Practical drafting: allocating rights in user-uploaded content, broadcast reuse, and creator protections

outline.chapter_title: Implied-in-Fact Contracts in Entertainment and Media Deals
outline.description: Covers formation and pleading of implied-in-fact contracts under New York law, the necessity of alleging essential terms and a meeting of the minds, and contrasts with classic idea-submission cases.
subtopics: New York standards: intent, surrounding circumstances, and mutual assent
Pleading essential terms: Caniglia and the requirement of specificity
Evidence of a meeting of the minds: DG & A and similar authorities
Rocky Point and scope of implied terms drawn from conduct and customs
Comparative note: Desny v. Wilder and idea-submission implied contracts
Application to Santos: failure to plead specific terms or assent to abide by platform TOS

outline.chapter_title: Fraudulent Inducement and the Out-of-Pocket Rule
outline.description: Explains the elements of fraudulent inducement under New York law and the distinctive damages measure that often defeats claims where plaintiffs received the agreed consideration.
subtopics: Elements of fraudulent inducement under New York law
Lama Holding and Connaughton: out-of-pocket loss versus benefit-of-the-bargain
Stings, pseudonyms, and deception in newsgathering and comedy: injury analysis
What qualifies as cognizable pecuniary loss and how to plead it
Application to Santos: no out-of-pocket loss where plaintiff was paid for requested work

outline.chapter_title: Ethics, Deception, and Fair Use: Beyond Doctrine
outline.description: Considers the normative and practical implications of using deception to obtain content for commentary, and the limited role that such conduct plays in fair use analysis after Supreme Court guidance.
subtopics: Harper & Row’s good-faith dictum revisited by Campbell and Google v. Oracle
Unclean hands and equitable defenses in copyright cases
Journalistic and comedic ethics versus legal permissibility
Risk management for media entities: reputation, audience trust, and litigation exposure
Guidelines for responsible use of pranks and stings in creative commentary

outline.chapter_title: Comparative Case Law and Adjacent Doctrines
outline.description: Situates Santos v. Kimmel within broader jurisprudence on transformative use, news reporting, and snippet/full-work copying, and touches on right of publicity and other non-copyright claims.
subtopics: Swatch v. Bloomberg: news reporting, complete copying, and market effects
Authors Guild v. Google Books: searchability, snippet view, and transformativeness
TCA Television v. McCollum and Cariou v. Prince: early-stage and visual art transformations
TVEyes and broadcast monitoring cases: functional uses and limits
Parody lineage: Campbell and its progeny; satire/commentary in modern media
Right of publicity overview and preemption intersections (brief note)

outline.description: Synthesizes the case’s doctrinal impact, offers strategic advice to creators, platforms, and media companies, and identifies unresolved questions for courts and litigants.
subtopics: Doctrinal takeaways: objective transformativeness, market-usurpation focus, and limited role of bad faith
Litigation strategies: positioning for or against early fair use adjudication
Platform drafting: making (or avoiding) third-party beneficiary rights explicit
Creator economy implications: personalized content, licensing expectations, and public-figure commentary
Open questions: boundaries of satire/commentary, platform-induced reliance, and evolving markets for critical uses

outline.description: Provides exercises to test understanding and explore how small factual changes could alter outcomes under fair use and state-law doctrines.
subtopics: What if the show aired the videos without commentary, in full, and monetized them exclusively on social platforms?
What if Santos included a visible license term or watermark restricting broadcast use in each video?
Would a narrowly tailored right of publicity claim avoid preemption and survive fair use in this context?
If Kimmel edited the videos to fabricate statements Santos did not make, how would that affect factors one and four?
Assume a detailed, mutually acknowledged message exchange agreeing to abide by TOS—does an implied-in-fact or express contract claim now lie?
What out-of-pocket loss could be plausibly alleged if Santos declined higher-paying requests due to time spent on Kimmel’s prompts?
